content: Community-based HIV testing services involve providing HIV testing outside of traditional healthcare facilities, directly within community settings. This approach was recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2013 to increase testing access, particularly for key populations such as young people, men, and individuals less likely to visit healthcare facilities. Community-based testing can be implemented in various ways, including fixed community sites, mobile outreach in hotspots like parks, bars, clubs, and workplaces, or even at people’s homes, often referred to as home-based testing. Home-based testing can be offered door-to-door or targeted to specific groups, such as partners of individuals living with HIV. These services are typically delivered by trained lay providers or peers using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and can be integrated with testing for other infections like tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). They may also be combined with broader community services, such as maternal and child health or family planning. Proper training and supervision of providers are essential when combining HIV testing with other services. WHO strongly recommends community-based HIV testing in high-burden settings, linking individuals to prevention, treatment, and care services. In low-burden settings, these services are particularly recommended for key populations. By 2019, 82% of reporting countries globally had adopted community-based HIV testing approaches. A systematic review of nearly 500 studies demonstrated that community-based testing effectively reaches individuals who might not otherwise test, with high uptake rates among both general and key populations. The review highlighted that community-based testing models vary in effectiveness depending on the population and setting. For example, workplace testing reached a high proportion of men (91%), while nearly half of those tested in the general population were first-time testers. Among key populations, 70% were first-time testers. The majority of individuals diagnosed through community-based testing were newly diagnosed, with linkage to treatment and care comparable to facility-based testing. Community-based testing can also be combined with testing for other infections, achieving high uptake rates, particularly when integrated with STI testing. However, uptake was lower when combined only with TB testing or other chronic conditions. Implementation considerations include timing and frequency of services, focusing on populations with unmet testing needs, and ensuring community engagement to enhance acceptance and effectiveness. Cost-effectiveness depends on factors such as local epidemiology and the populations reached. HIV self-testing (HIVST) has emerged as an additional approach to expand testing access. It allows individuals to collect their own specimens (oral fluid or blood), perform the test, and interpret the results privately. WHO first recommended HIVST in 2016, and its implementation has grown globally. A systematic review of 32 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found that HIVST significantly increased testing uptake compared to standard facility-based testing, with comparable rates of HIV positivity and linkage to care. Misuse and social harms associated with HIVST were rare, and the approach was found to be acceptable and feasible across diverse populations and settings. HIVST service delivery models include online or phone-based kit requests, distribution at facilities or community sites, and secondary distribution by individuals to their peers or partners. Support tools, such as tailored instructions, in-person demonstrations, or virtual support, can enhance the effectiveness of HIVST. Studies showed that HIVST increased testing uptake by 60% compared to standard testing, with high acceptability among users. Barriers to HIVST were minimal and included concerns about accuracy, user errors, and cost. Globally, the supply of HIVST products is strong, with several countries implementing or piloting HIVST programs. Lay users can reliably and accurately perform HIVST, achieving results comparable to those of trained healthcare workers. While the cost of HIVST is generally higher than facility-based testing, it is considered cost-effective in high-prevalence settings when focused on priority populations. Overall, community-based HIV testing and HIVST are effective strategies for reaching underserved populations, improving equity, and expanding access to HIV testing and care. These approaches are particularly valuable for key populations and individuals at ongoing risk of HIV, offering flexibility, privacy, and convenience while maintaining high levels of accuracy and safety.
